title: Mortgage Rates Near 7% as Fed Hike Squeezes Homebuyers Ahead of Midterms
excerpt: The 30-year fixed mortgage rate climbed to 6.95% this week, its highest since January 2025, as the Federal Reserve's first rate increase in three years snuffed out hopes of borrowing relief — pushing housing affordability to the center of the midterm debate.
body:
• Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 6.95%, up from 6.76% last week — the highest since January 2025 and the fourth consecutive weekly increase.
  • The jump landed a day after the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in three years, to a range of 3.75%–4.0%, and signaled another hike could follow before year-end.
  • Nearly half of the metropolitan areas tracked by the National Association of Realtors now require household income of at least $100,000 to afford a median-priced home with 10% down, up from just 6% of metros in 2019.
  • With midterm elections roughly seven weeks away, housing costs have become a defining affordability issue, pressuring both parties to answer for the squeeze.

Six weeks before the midterm elections, the cost of owning a home in America just got worse. Freddie Mac reported Thursday that the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate climbed to 6.95%, the highest since January 2025, when President Donald Trump returned to office. The fourth straight weekly rise came immediately after the Federal Reserve lifted its benchmark rate for the first time in three years, crushing any lingering hope that borrowing costs would ease soon.

The move lands on an electorate already feeling the strain at the grocery store, the gas pump, and the rent check. For millions of would-be buyers, the math has moved decisively out of reach: a borrower financing a typical $400,000 home now pays roughly $50 more each month than a week ago, and hundreds more than a year ago, when the average 30-year rate sat at 6.26%.

"It seems like we're trying to climb out of a hole somebody else is digging."

— A frustrated house hunter, quoted by CBS News

How We Got Here

The Federal Reserve's decision Wednesday was a quarter-point increase — its first since 2023 — lifting the benchmark rate to about 3.9% and opening the door to a second increase to 4.1% later this year. While the Fed does not set mortgage rates directly, its benchmark shapes the 10-year Treasury yield, which tracks 30-year mortgages. That yield is hovering near a high last seen in 2007, and mortgage pricing has marched higher with it.

The structural pressures go beyond the Fed. Heavy corporate borrowing tied to AI infrastructure buildouts is competing for capital in bond markets, and elevated energy costs since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February have kept inflation expectations high — national average gasoline prices remain roughly 94 cents higher than before the war, according to AAA data.

For homebuyers, this marks a return to territory that once felt like a distant ceiling. After rates dipped toward 6% earlier this year, they have marched steadily higher since mid-summer, and the market has frozen on both sides: buyers are priced out of payments up hundreds of dollars from a year ago, while existing owners — many holding mortgages under 4% — refuse to sell and give up cheap financing.

"The rate hike all but guarantees that mortgage rates will remain stuck at or above the 7% threshold, which creates a psychological and financial barrier that will sharply squeeze affordability and sideline even more prospective buyers."

— Lisa Sturtevant, chief economist at Bright MLS

The Affordability Math

The National Association of Realtors now says 49% of the metropolitan areas it monitors demand household income of at least $100,000 to qualify for a median-priced home with 10% down. In 2019, that was true of just 6% of metros. Builder sentiment has slid to its weakest since late 2022, weighed down by softer mortgage application volumes and elevated material costs.

The slowdown is bleeding into transactions. Existing-home sales are on track for a fifth straight annual decline, and pending home sales fell 4.7% from a year earlier in August. The silver lining: unsold inventory rose to a 4.9-month supply, a decade high, giving active shoppers their best negotiating position in years.

The Diaspora Angle

Indian-American homebuyers sit near the epicenter of this squeeze. The community is concentrated in high-cost metros — the Bay Area, New York, New Jersey, Seattle, and the Dallas suburbs — where median prices already demand six-figure qualifying incomes. For immigrants on work visas such as the H-1B, with limited job mobility, elevated rates plus record prices erode the confidence needed to commit to a mortgage.

What to Watch

The Fed's next moves are the single biggest variable. Another hike before year-end would lock in the 7% threshold the Bright MLS economist warned about, while any signal of pause could give rates room to drift lower. Watch the 10-year Treasury yield — the housing market's de facto thermostat — and both parties' first-time buyer proposals as the midterms approach.

For buyers still in the market, the playbook is patience and leverage: record inventory gives shoppers negotiating power unseen in a decade, and any relief in rates would bring sidelined demand flooding back. But as this week's data made clear, relief is not coming soon.
image_caption: A 'sold' sign outside a suburban American home. Mortgage rates near 7% are squeezing homebuyers ahead of the midterms.
nri_angle: Indian-American buyers, heavily concentrated in high-cost metros like the Bay Area, New York, and Seattle, face some of the nation's steepest affordability hurdles as rising rates combine with already-elevated home prices.
author: Diaspora Desk
